rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Live-demo beats survive a text read.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Chunk 1 'The demo you're about to see', line 11: 'In the other window, ... Claude answers *Saimaa.* Then the same second prompt as before. Claude suggests something Finnish: salmon, rye bread, meatballs.' — narrates the second window's full outcome. Four lines later, same chunk, line 15: 'Before you watch the second session run, take a guess. What will it suggest?' asks the reader to predict an answer the text already gave. This matches the compendium's own canonical failure almost verbatim ('Take a guess before you watch the second session run' — outcome narrated above the guess-line, same slide). Harm check: the guess is the chunk's one active-learning beat ('Your guess reveals what you already know about how this works, and what you're about to learn') and it is dead on arrival for a reader who read straight down — the predictive moment either does nothing or reads as patronising since the answer was already stated. Harm is actually present, not just rule-shape matched. Context for the orchestrator, not corrected here (out of this file's scope): the identical sentence at the identical line number exists in the sibling lecture curriculum/lectures/context-is-king.md (this file's own maintainer block names that file as Source), and that sibling's current slides instance (agents-101--lecture--context-is-king.slides.json) records rule 4 as N/A with the evidence 'no guess/predict-before-reveal instruction appears in the expanded body of curriculum/lectures/context-is-king.md' — which is not true of either file.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.

Three of four here are orientation-style labels rather than claims — 'The demo you're about to see' (chunk 1), 'What just happened' (chunk 2), 'The move you're about to make' (chunk 4) — each falls under the rule's own orientation-header carve-out (parallel to its named examples 'You are here'/'The far half opens': each announces a phase of the lecture rather than instructing a task). The fourth, 'Context isn't only about countries' (chunk 3), is a genuine declarative claim. No heading reads as exercise-style task-instruction anywhere, so the lecture mood stays consistent. Classified non-blocking per the template's stated principle: this is a mood/craft polish concern, not a comprehension failure — a reader follows the deck regardless of which headings are strict claims.
